q: A white building with sweeping curves carries fine ornament: scrolls, vines, shells, and light geometric patterning. Name the style.
n: White walls, sweeping curves, and scroll, vine, and shell decoration describe Rococo. Art Nouveau is the near miss because it also uses curved plant forms, but its shapes are asymmetrical and it came around 1890.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Rococo

q: Roughly what period does Rococo architecture span?
n: Rococo runs from 1650 to 1790 AD, inside the Baroque range of 1600 to 1830, because Rococo was Baroque's last phase.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Rococo

q: Roughly what period does Neoclassicism span?
n: Neoclassicism runs from 1730 to 1925 AD. Beaux Arts (1895 to 1925) ends in the same year, which is why the two ranges are easy to confuse.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Neoclassicism

q: Russian aristocrats worked Baroque ideas into the building of which city?
n: Peter the Great founded St. Petersburg in 1703, and Baroque architects such as Rastrelli built its Winter Palace. Moscow is the older capital and the usual wrong guess.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Baroque

q: Renewed interest in the ideas of which Renaissance architect inspired Neoclassicism?
n: Renewed interest in Palladio, spread by Lord Burlington and Palladian country houses in England, inspired the return of classical shapes. Palladio himself was a Renaissance architect, which links the two periods.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Neoclassicism

q: Rococo developed during the last phase of which style?
n: Rococo buildings came in the last phase of the Baroque period. Neoclassicism came after, and turned back toward classical shapes rather than ornament.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Rococo

q: Which period is known as an 'age of awakening' that brought back classical ideas?
n: The Renaissance returned to classical ideas and ushered in an age of awakening. Neoclassicism also revived classical shapes, but centuries later and inspired by the Renaissance itself.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Renaissance

q: In France, the highly ornamented Baroque style was combined with what?
n: French Baroque paired heavy ornament with Classical restraint, which set it apart from the extravagant Italian churches. Asymmetrical plant forms belong to Art Nouveau.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Baroque

q: Roughly what period does Baroque architecture span?
n: Baroque runs from 1600 to 1830 AD. The range 1650 to 1790 is Rococo, which sits inside the Baroque span as its last phase.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Baroque

q: Roughly what period does Renaissance architecture span?
n: The Renaissance runs from 1400 to 1600 AD, and Baroque picks up at 1600. The range 1730 to 1925 is Neoclassicism, the later return to Renaissance ideas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Renaissance

q: Which Renaissance architect looked to the classical orders of ancient Greece and Rome and wrote The Four Books of Architecture?
n: Andrea Palladio (1508–1580) published The Four Books of Architecture in 1570 and built villas such as the Villa Rotonda. Walter Gropius is the modernist behind the Bauhaus School.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Renaissance

q: How is the Baroque style in Italy best described?
o: Graceful white buildings with sweeping curves
Heavy ornament held in check by Classical restraint
Opulent, dramatic churches with irregular shapes and extravagant ornamentation
n: Italian Baroque is the opulent, dramatic, extravagantly ornamented version. Heavy ornament held in check by Classical restraint is how French Baroque differs from it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Baroque

q: Russian aristocrats brought Baroque ideas home after being impressed by which building?
n: Versailles in France is the building that impressed the Russian aristocracy. Hagia Sophia is Byzantine and Chartres is Gothic, so neither could have been a Baroque model.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Baroque

q: Neoclassicism spread classical shapes, proportioned by the classical orders, through which regions?
o: Europe, Great Britain, and the United States
n: Neoclassical buildings appeared in Europe, Great Britain, and the United States. Italy, France, and England is the Renaissance list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Neoclassicism

q: The Renaissance return to classical ideas took hold in which three countries?
o: Europe, Great Britain, and the United States
n: The Renaissance is placed in Italy, France, and England. Europe, Great Britain, and the United States is where Neoclassicism later spread classical shapes.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Renaissance

q: Which of these is NOT one of the modern-day trends that grew out of the Modernist style?
n: Art Moderne, the Bauhaus School, Deconstructivism, Formalism, and Structuralism all belong to the modern era. Classical Revival is another name for Beaux Arts, which looked back to Greece and Rome.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Modernist Style

q: Roughly what period does the Modernist style span?
n: The Modernist style runs from 1900 to the present. The range 1972 to the present belongs to Postmodernism, which reacted against it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Modernist Style

q: A building shows strict order, symmetry, formal design, grandiosity, and elaborate ornamentation. Which style fits best?
n: Order, symmetry, formality, grandiosity, and rich ornament are the Beaux Arts traits. Art Nouveau is the wrong pick because it rejects symmetry in favour of asymmetrical, flowing forms.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Beaux Arts

q: Roughly what period does Art Deco span?
n: Art Deco runs from 1925 to 1937, the jazz age. The range 1905 to 1930 is Neo-Gothic, the other style that dressed early skyscrapers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Deco

q: How did Postmodernism respond to the Modernist approach?
o: By reinventing historical details and familiar motifs
By stripping away every historical reference
By returning strictly to the Gothic cathedral
By limiting ornament to zigzags and vertical lines
n: Postmodern buildings reacted against Modernism by bringing back historical details and familiar motifs, so classical and ancient ideas show up in them again. Stripping away history is closer to what Modernism did.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Postmodernism

q: Which name is NOT given as another name for Beaux Arts architecture?
n: Beaux Arts is also called Beaux Arts Classicism, Academic Classicism, or Classical Revival. Neo-Gothic is a separate style that revived medieval details, not classical ones.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Beaux Arts

q: Which architect founded the Bauhaus School?
n: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 and led it until 1928. Le Corbusier was a leading Modernist too, but he never taught at the Bauhaus.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Modernist Style

q: Before it reached architecture and furniture in the 1890s, where was Art Nouveau first expressed?
n: Art Nouveau began in fabrics and graphic design, then spread to architecture and furniture in the 1890s.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Nouveau

q: Roughly what period does Beaux Arts span?
n: Beaux Arts runs from 1895 to 1925. Neoclassicism also ends in 1925 but began much earlier, in 1730.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Beaux Arts

q: Roughly what period does Neo-Gothic skyscraper design span?
n: Neo-Gothic runs from 1905 to 1930. The range 1100 to 1450 is the original Gothic period whose details it borrowed.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Neo-Gothic

q: Art Nouveau is also known by what name?
n: Art Nouveau is French for 'New Art', and the style is also called the New Style. Art Moderne is a later streamlined offshoot of Art Deco, and Classical Revival is another name for Beaux Arts.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Nouveau

q: Jazz-age Art Deco buildings are known for which visual effect?
n: Zigzag patterns and vertical lines give Art Deco its dramatic look. Asymmetrical plant-like surfaces are Art Nouveau, the style Art Deco followed.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Deco

q: Roughly what period does Art Nouveau span?
n: Art Nouveau runs from 1890 to 1914. The range 1895 to 1925 is Beaux Arts, which started at almost the same time.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Nouveau

q: Which features mark Art Nouveau buildings?
o: Scrolls, vines, and shells on white walls
Zigzag patterns and strong vertical lines
Asymmetrical shapes, arches, and curved, plant-like decoration
n: Art Nouveau buildings have asymmetrical shapes, arches, and curved, plant-like surfaces. Scrolls, vines, and shells on white walls are Rococo, which also uses curves but keeps them delicate and symmetrical.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Nouveau

q: Roughly what period does Postmodernism span?
n: Postmodernism starts in 1972 and continues to the present. The Modernist style it reacted against starts earlier, in 1900.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Postmodernism

q: Art Deco designers borrowed a great deal of their ornament from one ancient civilisation. Which one?
n: Howard Carter's discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922 set off an 'Egyptomania' that filled Art Deco with Egyptian motifs.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Art Deco

q: An early 20th-century skyscraper is ornamented with gargoyles, arched windows, and other medieval details. Which style is it?
n: Neo-Gothic applied Gothic details to modern buildings, including soaring skyscrapers. Gothic proper ended by 1450, centuries before skyscrapers existed.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Neo-Gothic

q: Roughly what period does Classical (Greek and Roman) architecture span?
n: Classical architecture runs from 850 BC to 476 AD, ending with the fall of Rome. The year 330 AD is when Constantine moved the capital to Byzantium, not the end of the Classical period.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Classical

q: The Classical period runs from the rise of ancient Greece until which event?
o: Constantine moving the capital to Byzantium
The fall of the Roman Empire
n: Classical architecture spans the rise of Greece to the fall of the Roman Empire, which is why its range ends at 476 AD. Constantine's move in 330 AD happened while the empire still stood.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Classical

q: Byzantine builders mostly used which material in place of stone?
n: Byzantine builders favoured thin fired brick laid in thick mortar, as in Hagia Sophia. Concrete is more closely tied to Roman building, the style Byzantine grew out of.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Byzantine

q: Roughly what period does Gothic architecture span?
n: Gothic runs from 1100 to 1450 AD. The range 1905 to 1930 belongs to Neo-Gothic, the 20th-century revival of Gothic details.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Gothic

q: Roughly what period does Romanesque architecture span?
n: Romanesque runs from 800 to 1200 AD. Gothic starts at 1100 AD, so the two overlap for about a century.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Romanesque

q: In what year did Constantine move the capital of the Roman Empire to Byzantium?
n: Constantine moved the capital in 330 AD, and Roman architecture there evolved into the Byzantine style. 476 AD is the fall of Rome, which closes the Classical period.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Byzantine

q: A medieval town has a cathedral with pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses. Its older castle has rounded arches and heavy piers. Which styles are they?
n: Pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses are Gothic. Rounded arches with heavy piers are Romanesque, which fits an older building because Romanesque (800 to 1200 AD) came first.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Romanesque and Gothic

q: Chartres and Notre Dame are famous cathedrals in which style?
n: Gothic ideas produced magnificent cathedrals like Chartres and Notre Dame. Neo-Gothic is the 20th-century revival that put Gothic details on skyscrapers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Gothic

q: Early Medieval churches and castles built with thick walls and heavy piers belong to which style?
n: Thick walls and heavy piers carry the load in Romanesque churches and castles. Gothic replaced that mass with flying buttresses and ribbed vaults.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Romanesque

q: Domed roofs, elaborate mosaics, and classical forms together identify which style?
n: These are the Byzantine traits, along with brick in place of stone. Romanesque is the near miss for a church, but its markers are rounded arches, thick walls, and heavy piers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Byzantine

q: Greek and Roman buildings were built according to precise rules. Which system set their column styles and entablature designs?
n: The Classical Orders fixed the column style and the entablature above it, and they still shape building design today. Flying buttresses and ribbed vaulting are Gothic structural inventions, not rules of proportion.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Classical

q: Which set of innovations allowed Gothic buildings to become taller and more graceful?
o: Rounded arches, thick walls, and heavy piers
Domed roofs, brick walls, and mosaics
Pointed arches, ribbed vaulting, and flying buttresses
Zigzag patterns and strong vertical lines
n: Pointed arches, ribbed vaulting, and flying buttresses spread the loads so walls could rise higher and thinner. Rounded arches with thick walls and heavy piers describe Romanesque, the style Gothic moved beyond.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Gothic

q: The golden age of Byzantine architecture, under Emperor Justinian I, spans which years?
n: 527 to 565 AD is the reign of Emperor Justinian I, the golden age of Byzantine building that produced Hagia Sophia (537). The range 800 to 1200 AD is Romanesque, and 330 AD is the year Constantine moved the capital.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Byzantine

q: Of these styles, which began earliest?
n: Byzantine starts in 527 AD, ahead of Romanesque (800 AD), Gothic (1100 AD), and Renaissance (1400 AD).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline

q: Byzantium, the city Constantine made the new Roman capital, is known today by what name?
n: Byzantium is now Istanbul. Ravenna holds famous Byzantine mosaics, which makes it a tempting pick, but it was never renamed from Byzantium.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Byzantine

q: As Rome's influence spread across Europe, a heavy, stocky style emerged. Which arch shape marks it?
n: Romanesque architecture is heavier and stockier, with rounded arches. The pointed arch is the Gothic answer, and it is what let later churches rise taller.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Romanesque

q: Mesopotamian architecture is also described by which regional name?
n: Mesopotamian building is also called West Asiatic architecture, after its region in western Asia. Byzantine is a later style from Constantinople, not the name for the Twin Rivers region.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Mesopotamia

q: The Pyramids of Giza prove that Egyptian building was far from primitive. What do they show?
o: Engineering able to reach great heights
The earliest use of the classical orders
The first use of fired brick in place of stone
n: The Great Pyramid of Khufu rose about 146 m and stayed the world's tallest structure for nearly 4,000 years. Brick in place of stone and domed roofs are Byzantine traits, and the classical orders come from Greece and Rome.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Ancient Egypt

q: Which kind of prehistoric structure has been lost to time?
n: Thatch and mud decay, so those buildings are gone. Stone circles, megaliths, and cliff dwellings were built of rock and survive, which is why examples like Stonehenge can still be named.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Prehistoric

q: Before there was any written record, which group of works were people already building?
o: Earthen mounds, stone circles, and megaliths
n: Earthen mounds, stone circles, and megaliths are the earliest monumental building, raised long before writing, and many still puzzle archaeologists. Pyramids, temples, and shrines came later, from the rulers of ancient Egypt.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Prehistoric

q: Powerful rulers of Ancient Egypt built which three kinds of monument?
n: Egypt's pharaohs built monumental pyramids, temples, and shrines, from Djoser's Step Pyramid to the temples of Karnak. Megaliths, mounds, and stone circles are prehistoric works.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Ancient Egypt

q: Stonehenge and the cliff dwellings of the Americas are grouped under which period?
n: Stonehenge in England and the cliff dwellings of the American Southwest were built by peoples without writing, which makes them prehistoric. Mesopotamia is the nearest wrong pick, but it names the architecture of Persia, Assyria, and Babylon, not megalithic Britain or the Americas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Prehistoric

q: Mesopotamian architecture grew up in the land of the 'Twin Rivers'. Which rivers are these?
n: Mesopotamia means the land between the Tigris and Euphrates. The Nile is Egypt's river, a common mix-up because both are early river civilisations.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Mesopotamia

q: Roughly what period does the architecture of Ancient Egypt span?
n: Ancient Egypt runs from 3,050 BC to 900 BC. The range 850 BC to 476 AD belongs to Classical (Greek and Roman) architecture, which begins just after Egypt's range ends.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Ancient Egypt

q: Mesopotamian architecture covers which group of civilisations?
n: Persia, Assyria, and Babylon are the civilisations grouped under Mesopotamia. Greece, Rome, and Byzantium belong to the Classical and Byzantine rows instead.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 1 — Timeline: Mesopotamia
